chunks: Biasing an amplifier. The question: How to bias an amplifier?
Biasing means setting a transistor's steady (DC) voltages and current so that a signal can swing up and down without being clipped.
You choose a resting point, usually near the middle of the available voltage range. The signal then moves around that point.
A good bias also stays put when the transistor's properties change.
Picture a swing at rest hanging from its chains. If you want it to move equally forward and backward, it should start at the center.
Starting at the far edge means it can only go one way. The bias is the resting position of the swing, and the signal is the push on top.
R 1 over R 2 fix the base at about 1. 65 volts; R E sets the emitter current; R C puts the collector near 7 volts.
C 1 and C 2 couple the signal in and out while blocking DC; C E bypasses R E at signal frequencies.
Bias / operating point (Q-point): the DC voltages and current when no signal is applied. Headroom: the room the signal has to swing before it clips.
Voltage-divider bias: two resistors that set the base voltage. Emitter resistor ( R E ): turns the emitter voltage into a stable emitter current.
Negative feedback: a self-correcting effect that holds the current steady.
Take a BJT, where a small base current controls the current from collector to emitter. Use a 12 volts supply and aim for 1 milliamps. Choose R E equals 1 kilohms.
The emitter sits at 1 milliamps times 1 kilohms equals 1 volts, so the base sits about 0. 65 volts higher, at about 1. 65 volts. A divider holds the base there.
A 5 kilohms collector resistor drops 5 volts, so the collector rests at 12-5 equals 7 volts. If the current tries to rise, the emitter voltage rises and pulls it back.
That is the whole idea.
"Biasing sets the DC operating point so the transistor stays active and the signal can swing symmetrically.

For a BJT I use voltage-divider bias with an emitter resistor: the divider sets the base voltage, I E equals (V B-V BE) over R E , so the current depends on resistors, not on beta , and the emitter resistor gives negative DC feedback.
The divider current is about ten times the base current, and the collector sits near mid-supply. Coupling capacitors pass the signal, and a bypass capacitor restores gain.
For a MOSFET it's a gate divider with a source resistor, and for an op-amp on a single supply the input sits at half the rail."
